posts.title: Semantic Caching: Reusing Answers to Similar Prompts
posts.subtitle: Cosine similarity turns 'close enough' questions into free cache hits
posts.summary: Semantic caching stores LLM responses keyed by the embedding of the prompt, not its exact text, so a rephrased question can still hit the cache. It cuts cost and latency on high-traffic apps, but the similarity threshold is a real dial: too loose and you serve wrong answers, too strict and you barely cache anything.

slides.title: Most Prompts Are Rephrasings of Ones You've Already Answered
slides.body: A support bot, a docs assistant, a search feature — most production LLM traffic is the same handful of questions asked in slightly different words.
bullets: Exact-match caching only catches identical strings
Users rarely type the exact same sentence twice
Every near-duplicate still pays full LLM latency and cost

slides.title: Exact-Match Caching Misses the Point
slides.body: "What's the capital of France?" and "France's capital city?" are the same question — but a hash-the-literal-string cache treats them as completely unrelated.
bullets: Hash-based caches only hit on byte-identical prompts
Whitespace, punctuation, or word order alone breaks a hit
Real user traffic is far too varied for exact matching to help much

slides.title: Cache by Meaning, Not by String
slides.body: Embed the incoming query, then compare it against the embeddings of previously-answered queries using cosine similarity. Above a threshold, return the cached answer instead of calling the model.
bullets: Embed query → look up nearest neighbors in a vector index
If similarity ≥ threshold (commonly ~0.92–0.97) → cache hit, return stored response
If below threshold → cache miss, call the LLM, store the new pair

slides.title: The Pipeline in Four Steps
bullets: 1. Embed the incoming prompt with a fast embedding model
2. Approximate-nearest-neighbor lookup (e.g. HNSW) against cached query embeddings
3. Score the closest match; compare to the similarity threshold
4. Hit → return cached response; Miss → call the LLM, embed and store the new pair

slides.title: A Support Bot at Scale
slides.body: Picture a support bot handling a large daily volume of questions, where a meaningful share are near-duplicates of ones it has already answered — 'How do I reset my password?' vs 'password reset steps?' vs 'I forgot my password, help.'
bullets: Without semantic caching: every one of those is a fresh, full-price LLM call
With a well-tuned threshold: the near-duplicates hit the cache and skip the model entirely
The savings scale with how repetitive the traffic actually is — measure it, don't assume it

slides.title: Exact-Match vs. Semantic Cache

rows: Can serve a wrong answer to a near-but-different question

slides.title: The Threshold Is the Whole Game
slides.body: Set it too loose and the cache confidently returns a wrong answer to a subtly different question. Set it too strict and you've built infrastructure that barely ever fires.
bullets: Too loose: 'cancel my order' and 'cancel my account' can drift dangerously close in embedding space
Too strict: real paraphrases fall just outside the cutoff and you gain almost nothing
Stale cache: an answer that was correct yesterday (price, status, policy) can be wrong today even for the exact same question

slides.title: When to Reach for It — and When Not To
slides.body: Semantic caching earns its keep on high-volume, repetitive, low-stakes queries. It's the wrong tool when correctness matters more than cost.
bullets: Good fit: FAQ-style support, docs search, autocomplete-style assistance
Bad fit: medical, legal, or financial answers where a near-miss is unacceptable
Always pair with a TTL or invalidation strategy for anything that can go stale

questions.prompt: Why does exact-match caching perform poorly on real LLM traffic?
options: It's too slow to look up
Users rarely type byte-identical prompts, even when asking the same question
It requires a vector database
It only works for single-word queries
questions.explanation: Exact-match caching hashes the literal prompt string, so any rephrasing — different word order, punctuation, or wording — misses the cache even though the underlying question is identical.

questions.prompt: What determines whether an incoming query is a semantic cache hit?
options: Whether it was asked more than once before
The length of the prompt
Cosine similarity between the query's embedding and cached query embeddings, compared to a threshold
Whether the same user sent it previously
questions.explanation: The incoming prompt is embedded and compared against stored query embeddings; if the similarity score clears the configured threshold, the cached response is returned instead of calling the model.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of setting the similarity threshold too low?
options: The cache uses too much memory
The cache serves a confidently wrong answer to a question that only looks similar to a cached one
The embedding model becomes slower
It disables the vector index entirely
questions.explanation: A threshold that's too permissive lets meaningfully different questions — like 'cancel my order' vs 'cancel my account' — count as a match, so the cache returns an answer to the wrong question.

posts.title: Reranking: The Second-Stage Filter RAG Forgets
posts.subtitle: Vector search finds candidates fast; a reranker decides which ones actually answer the question
posts.summary: Bi-encoder vector search is fast because it embeds queries and documents independently and precomputes the index, but that independence is also its weakness: it never lets the query and document actually attend to each other. A cross-encoder reranker fixes this by scoring the query and each candidate jointly, and is added as a cheap-to-expensive second stage that reorders a small shortlist rather than the whole corpus.

slides.title: Fast and Right Are Different Jobs
slides.body: A vector index can hand back the top 100 candidates for a query in milliseconds. It's much worse at telling you which one of those 100 is actually the best answer. Reranking is the stage that fixes that.

slides.title: Bi-encoders never let query and document meet
slides.body: A standard vector retriever (a bi-encoder) embeds the query and every document separately, ahead of time, then compares the two vectors with cosine similarity or dot product at query time.
bullets: That separation is what makes vector search fast: document embeddings are precomputed once and stored in an ANN index, so a query only needs one new embedding plus a nearest-neighbor lookup
But the model never sees the query and a specific document together -- it can't let query tokens attend to document tokens, so it can't judge fine-grained relevance the way a reader would
The result: the top-k list is a reasonable shortlist, but the ordering within it is often noisy -- a document that's topically close but doesn't actually answer the question can outrank one that does

slides.title: Score query and document together, on a shortlist
slides.body: A cross-encoder reranker concatenates the query and one candidate document into a single input and runs the pair through a transformer jointly, so every query token can attend to every document token before producing one relevance score.
bullets: Because it needs both the query and the document at inference time, a cross-encoder can't be precomputed -- it must run a fresh forward pass for every query-document pair, so it never runs over a whole corpus directly

The fix is a two-stage pipeline: a cheap bi-encoder (or hybrid/BM25) retrieves a wide candidate set -- commonly the top 50 to a few hundred -- and the cross-encoder reranks only that shortlist down to the top 5-10 actually sent to the LLM

Some stacks swap the cross-encoder for an LLM-as-reranker: prompt a language model to score or rank the shortlist directly. More accurate on nuanced queries, but noticeably slower and costlier per candidate than a purpose-built cross-encoder

slides.title: Walking through one query
slides.body: Query: 'How do I cancel a subscription mid-cycle and get a prorated refund?' The vector index returns three candidates in this order.
bullets: #1 from vector search: a general 'Managing Your Subscription' FAQ page -- high embedding similarity because it shares lots of subscription-related vocabulary, but never mentions refunds
#2 from vector search: 'Prorated Refunds for Mid-Cycle Cancellations' -- the actual answer, but ranked lower because its wording overlaps less with the query on the surface
#3 from vector search: a billing-cycle explainer with no cancellation content at all

The cross-encoder reads the query jointly with each candidate and correctly promotes #2 to the top -- it can recognize that 'cancel mid-cycle' + 'prorated refund' is directly addressed there, something cosine similarity on separate embeddings couldn't weigh precisely

slides.title: Two different jobs in the pipeline
slides.body: Bi-encoders and cross-encoders trade accuracy for scale in opposite directions -- that's exactly why production systems use both, in sequence, rather than picking one.

rows: Encoded jointly, with attention between them
No -- runs fresh per query-document pair
Small shortlist only (tens to a few hundred)

slides.title: Where reranking stops paying for itself
slides.body: A second stage is not free -- it adds latency and a new model to maintain, and it isn't always the bottleneck worth fixing.
bullets: Every candidate you rerank costs one more forward pass; reranking a shortlist of a few hundred documents with a heavier model can add a meaningful chunk of end-to-end latency to a request that otherwise felt instant

If the first-stage retriever already has strong recall and a clean top-k (small, well-separated corpus, narrow domain), the reranker mostly reorders documents that were already fine -- added cost for little quality gain

Rerankers are trained on general-purpose relevance data; a reranker that hasn't seen your domain's vocabulary (internal jargon, legal or medical terms) can misjudge relevance just as confidently as it judges correctly elsewhere

Reranking corrects ordering within the shortlist -- it cannot recover a genuinely relevant document that the first-stage retriever failed to surface at all. Bad recall upstream still needs fixing upstream

slides.title: Retrieve wide, rerank narrow
slides.body: Reranking is the standard second stage in production RAG for a reason: it's precision applied exactly where it's affordable.
bullets: Use a fast bi-encoder (optionally fused with BM25/hybrid search) to pull a wide candidate set with high recall, then a cross-encoder to reorder that set with high precision
The shortlist size is the main knob: too narrow and the reranker never sees the right answer; too wide and latency creeps up for little extra gain
Skip reranking when your corpus is small and clean enough that the first-stage ranking is already reliable, or when the latency budget genuinely can't absorb another model call
A reranker fixes ordering, not recall -- pair it with good chunking and a retriever tuned for your domain rather than treating it as a cure-all

questions.prompt: Why can't a cross-encoder reranker be precomputed the way a bi-encoder's document embeddings can?
options: Cross-encoders only work on short documents
It needs the query and a specific document together as input, so there's nothing to embed ahead of time
Cross-encoders don't use transformers
It's a licensing restriction, not a technical one
questions.explanation: A cross-encoder concatenates the query and one document and runs them jointly through the model, so the score only exists once you know both. That's exactly why it's applied to a small shortlist at query time instead of the whole corpus.

questions.prompt: A RAG pipeline's vector search already has excellent recall on a small, narrow-domain corpus. What does adding a reranker mostly buy you here?
options: A large accuracy jump, since reranking always transforms results dramatically
Little benefit -- the candidates were already well-ordered, so reordering them adds latency for small gain
Nothing changes recall, but reranking will always be free
It replaces the need for a vector index entirely
questions.explanation: Reranking's value comes from fixing noisy ordering in a large, imprecise shortlist. If the first-stage retriever is already precise on a small, well-separated corpus, there's less noise to fix, so the extra model call costs latency without much quality upside.

questions.prompt: A relevant document never appears in the top 100 results returned by the first-stage retriever. Will a cross-encoder reranker fix this?
options: Yes, cross-encoders can recover any relevant document regardless of the first stage
No -- the reranker only reorders candidates it's given; it can't rank a document it never sees
Yes, but only if the document is very short
No, because cross-encoders never change document order
questions.explanation: Reranking operates strictly on the shortlist handed to it by the first-stage retriever. A recall failure upstream -- the right document never making the candidate set -- has to be fixed in retrieval (better chunking, hybrid search, larger k), not in reranking.

posts.title: LSM Trees: Why Modern Databases Write Sequentially
posts.subtitle: The write-optimized storage engine behind Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB
posts.summary: B-trees update pages in place, which turns every write into a random disk I/O once data outgrows RAM. Log-Structured Merge trees buffer writes in memory and flush them as sorted, immutable files, turning writes sequential -- at the cost of extra work later during compaction and reads. That single tradeoff explains the storage engine choice behind Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, and HBase.

slides.title: Trade Random Writes for Sequential Ones
slides.body: A B-tree updates a record by rewriting its page in place, wherever that page happens to sit on disk. An LSM tree never does that -- it only ever appends. That one decision reshapes everything about how the engine reads, writes, and reclaims space.

slides.title: In-Place Updates Make Every Write a Random Seek
slides.body: The bottleneck isn't CPU -- it's where on disk the write has to land.
bullets: A B-tree write touches whichever leaf page holds that key, and once the working set outgrows RAM cache, that page is somewhere random on disk
A random seek costs orders of magnitude more than a sequential write on spinning disks, and even on SSDs random writes trigger extra erase-block reshuffling internally
High-ingest workloads -- metrics, event logs, sensor streams, time series -- generate far more write volume than a random-I/O-bound engine can absorb before it falls behind

slides.title: Buffer in Memory, Flush as Sorted Immutable Files
slides.body: An LSM tree defers the disk write and batches it.
bullets: Every write lands first in an in-memory sorted structure (the memtable, typically a skip list) and is appended to a write-ahead log on disk for crash durability
When the memtable fills -- commonly a 64MB-256MB threshold -- it's flushed to disk as one large sequential write: an immutable Sorted String Table (SSTable) that is never modified again

A read has to check the memtable first, then potentially several SSTables from newest to oldest -- each SSTable carries a Bloom filter so the engine can skip files that provably don't contain the key without touching disk

slides.title: Compaction Is What Keeps Reads From Degrading
slides.body: Left alone, SSTables pile up and a single read would need to check dozens of them -- compaction merges files back down.
bullets: Leveled compaction (RocksDB and LevelDB's default): SSTables are organized into levels L0 through L6, each roughly 10x larger than the one above; a key gets rewritten as it's pushed down levels, which favors low read and space amplification at the cost of extra write work

Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra's default, in the Bigtable lineage): similarly-sized SSTables are merged together as they accumulate; this keeps write amplification lower but lets more duplicate/stale data coexist, so space amplification is higher

Compaction is a background process competing for the same CPU and disk bandwidth as live traffic -- if it can't keep up, SSTables accumulate faster than they're merged ('compaction debt') and read latency climbs

slides.title: The Tradeoff, Side by Side
slides.body: Neither structure is strictly better -- each optimizes for a different access pattern.

rows: Higher -- compaction rewrites keys multiple times as they move through levels
Memtable plus possibly several SSTables, narrowed by Bloom filters
Higher until compaction reclaims stale/overwritten versions
Write-heavy, high-ingest workloads (Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, HBase)

slides.title: 50,000 Sensors Writing Once a Second
slides.body: A fleet of IoT sensors each writes a reading every second -- 50k small writes/sec, scattered across an effectively random key space.
bullets: On a B-tree engine, that's 50k potential random page touches per second -- disk IOPS becomes the bottleneck long before storage capacity does

On an LSM engine (this is Cassandra's write path), every write instead lands in the memtable plus the append-only commit log; the memtable flushes to a brand-new SSTable every few minutes as a single sequential write, regardless of how scattered the actual keys were

Reading the latest value for one sensor checks the memtable first (fast, in RAM), then consults each SSTable's Bloom filter -- with a well-tuned false-positive rate around 1%, almost all irrelevant SSTables are skipped without a single disk read

slides.title: When an LSM Tree Is the Wrong Choice
slides.body: The write optimization isn't free, and sometimes it buys you nothing.
bullets: Read-heavy, point-lookup-dominated workloads with light write volume gain little from the write optimization while still paying its read and space overhead -- a plain B-tree is simpler and often faster there
Range scans across many un-compacted SSTables with overlapping key ranges can be slower than a B-tree's contiguous leaf pages
Space amplification means an LSM store can temporarily consume well over the logical data size until compaction catches up -- a real capacity-planning concern, not just a theoretical one
Under sustained write rates that outpace compaction throughput, read latency degrades sharply as unmerged SSTables accumulate -- a failure mode that doesn't exist for a B-tree

slides.title: Pick the Engine That Matches Your Write Pattern
slides.body: The whole design comes down to when you pay the I/O cost: at write time, or later.
bullets: LSM trees convert random writes into sequential ones by buffering in memory and flushing sorted, immutable files -- the mechanism behind Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, and HBase
The cost shows up later: read amplification (multiple files to check per read) and write amplification (compaction rewrites data multiple times over its lifetime)
Leveled compaction trades more write amplification for better read/space efficiency; size-tiered compaction trades more space for better write throughput
Default to a B-tree for read-heavy or balanced OLTP; reach for an LSM-based engine when ingest volume, not lookup speed, is the binding constraint

questions.prompt: What's the core trick an LSM tree uses to avoid random disk writes?
options: It stores all data permanently in RAM
It buffers writes in memory and flushes them as sorted, immutable files in one sequential write
It uses a B-tree internally but caches more aggressively
It writes directly to raw SSD blocks using TRIM commands
questions.explanation: An LSM tree defers writing to disk until a memtable fills, then flushes the whole thing as one sequential file (an SSTable) instead of updating scattered pages in place -- that's what turns random writes into sequential ones.

questions.prompt: Why does an LSM tree rely on Bloom filters?
options: To compress SSTables on disk
To encrypt data before compaction
To quickly rule out SSTables that can't contain a given key, without reading them from disk
To decide which compaction strategy to run
questions.explanation: Since a read may need to check many SSTables, a Bloom filter per SSTable lets the engine skip files that provably don't contain the key, avoiding wasted disk I/O. False positives just cost an extra unnecessary check -- they never cause a missed key.

questions.prompt: Which workload is an LSM tree's design NOT a great fit for?
options: High-volume sensor or event ingestion
A write-heavy, append-mostly log
A read-heavy workload dominated by point lookups on rarely-changing data
Time-series data ingestion
questions.explanation: LSM trees pay their compaction and multi-file-read tax specifically to optimize writes. A workload that's mostly reads on rarely-changing data gets little of that benefit while still paying the read and space amplification costs -- a plain B-tree is usually simpler and faster there.

posts.title: Hybrid Search: When Keyword Beats a Perfect Embedding
posts.subtitle: Why every serious RAG stack still runs BM25 next to the vector index
posts.summary: Dense vector search is great at meaning but bad at exact tokens -- SKUs, error codes, acronyms, rare proper nouns -- because embeddings compress them into the same neighborhood as similar-sounding words. Hybrid search fixes this by running a sparse keyword ranker (BM25) alongside the dense retriever and fusing the two rankings, typically with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so exact matches and semantic matches both surface.

slides.title: Two Retrievers Are Better Than One
slides.body: Pure vector search quietly fails on the exact strings people actually search for -- part numbers, error codes, names. Hybrid search runs a keyword ranker alongside the embedding search and merges the results.

slides.title: Embeddings blur the tokens that matter most
slides.body: A dense embedding model maps text into a continuous space optimized for semantic similarity. That's exactly the property that breaks exact-match retrieval.
bullets: Query 'error E4021' can rank a doc about 'error E4029' above the one that actually contains E4021 -- the embedding sees them as nearly identical
Rare proper nouns, product SKUs, and acronyms often collapse into the same neighborhood as unrelated but stylistically similar text
Embedding models are trained on general semantic similarity, not on your domain's exact-identifier vocabulary

slides.title: Run a sparse ranker in parallel, then fuse
slides.body: BM25 (a term-frequency / inverse-document-frequency ranking function) scores documents by exact and near-exact term overlap -- the opposite failure mode of dense embeddings. Hybrid search runs both retrievers on the same query and merges their result lists.
bullets: BM25 rewards documents where the query's exact terms appear, weighted by how rare those terms are across the corpus
The two rankers produce scores on incompatible scales, so you can't just add them -- you need a fusion step
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps the scaling problem entirely by fusing on RANK, not raw score: score(d) = sum over rankers of 1 / (k + rank(d)), with k commonly set around 60

slides.title: Walking through one query
slides.body: Query: 'reset procedure for E4021'. The corpus has a runbook titled 'E4021 Reset Procedure' and a semantically similar but wrong doc titled 'E4029 Recovery Steps'.
bullets: Dense retriever: ranks 'E4029 Recovery Steps' #1 (semantically close: both are error-reset docs) and buries the correct E4021 doc at #6
BM25: ranks the correct 'E4021 Reset Procedure' #1 because the exact token 'E4021' matches, and ranks the E4029 doc much lower
RRF fusion: the correct doc gets 1/(60+1) from BM25 plus a smaller contribution from dense, pushing it back to the top of the merged list

slides.title: Each retriever covers the other's blind spot
slides.body: Neither ranker is strictly better -- they fail on different query shapes, which is exactly why fusing them helps instead of just picking the stronger one.

slides.title: Where hybrid search bites back
slides.body: Fusion isn't free -- it adds infrastructure, latency, and a new tuning surface.
bullets: You now run and maintain two indexes (inverted index + vector index) instead of one, doubling storage and indexing pipelines
Query latency is the max of two retrieval calls plus the fusion step, not just one -- matters under tight p99 budgets
RRF's k constant and any per-ranker weighting still need tuning per corpus; a k tuned for short product docs may hurt on long-form technical text
For small corpora (a few thousand docs) where BM25 alone already gets near-perfect recall, the added complexity may not pay for itself

slides.title: Default to hybrid unless you've measured otherwise
slides.body: Most production RAG systems that handle real user queries -- not just clean benchmark questions -- end up needing both signal types.
bullets: Pure dense search silently loses exact-match queries; pure keyword search silently loses paraphrased queries -- hybrid loses neither
Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the default fusion method because it needs no score normalization, only rank position
Pair hybrid retrieval with a reranker (cross-encoder) as a second-stage filter for best precision on the fused candidate set
Skip the complexity only when your corpus and query patterns are narrow enough that one retriever already covers both cases

questions.prompt: Why can't you just add raw BM25 and vector similarity scores together?
options: BM25 only works on English text
The two scores live on different, incompatible scales
Vector databases don't return numeric scores
BM25 scores are always higher than cosine similarity
questions.explanation: BM25 scores are unbounded term-weighted sums while cosine similarity is bounded roughly [-1,1] -- adding them directly lets whichever scale is numerically larger dominate. That's why rank-based fusion methods like RRF are used instead of raw score addition.

questions.prompt: A user searches for an exact error code like 'E4021'. Which retriever is most likely to surface the right document?
options: Dense vector search, because it understands meaning
BM25 keyword search, because it rewards exact rare-term matches
Neither -- exact codes can't be retrieved by either method
Only a reranker can find exact codes
questions.explanation: BM25's IDF weighting gives rare exact tokens like error codes a very high score when they match, while dense embeddings tend to blur near-identical codes into the same neighborhood. This is the core failure mode hybrid search is built to fix.

questions.prompt: What does Reciprocal Rank Fusion actually fuse on?
options: The raw similarity scores from each retriever
The document's position (rank) in each retriever's result list
The length of the document
The embedding vectors directly, via averaging
questions.explanation: RRF computes score(d) = sum of 1/(k + rank(d)) across each ranker's result list, using only rank position -- never the raw score. That's what makes it robust to two rankers whose scores are on completely different scales.

posts.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't
posts.subtitle: 8,135 trials say skills anchor behavior, not inject facts
posts.summary: A Princeton/Stanford/USC/Johns Hopkins team open-coded 8,135 agent trial records to answer a question nobody had actually tested: do 'skills' -- packaged procedures agents load at inference time -- help by teaching the model facts, or by stabilizing how it acts? The answer is procedural anchoring 65.7% of the time versus explicit knowledge injection only 4.5% of the time, and a real retrieval bottleneck emerges once skill libraries grow past a handful of entries.

slides.title: Skills Work by Anchoring Behavior, Not Injecting Facts
slides.body: Agent 'skills' -- SKILL.md-style procedures loaded at inference time -- have quietly become the default way to make LLM agents more reliable. This paper is the first large-scale, evidence-based look at why they actually work, and where they quietly stop.

slides.title: The default assumption was never actually tested
slides.body: Most teams write skills assuming they work like a mini fine-tune: they teach the agent something it didn't know. Nobody had systematically checked whether that's true across real trials.
bullets: Skills are usually pitched as knowledge injection -- filling gaps in what the base model knows
Practitioners write increasingly detailed SKILL.md files on that assumption, without evidence it's the right one
The authors normalized 8,135 trial records from controlled agent experiments to open-code what a skill actually changed

slides.title: Open-coding thousands of trials into a taxonomy
slides.body: From 8,135 normalized trial records, the authors retained 240 open-coded records that reduced to 238 valid unique labels, then built a taxonomy of 3 high-level categories and 12 concrete skill-use modes describing exactly how a skill changed agent behavior in each trial.
bullets: Categories span things like procedural anchoring, explicit knowledge injection, and error-recovery guidance
Each trial pairs a 'skill on' and 'skill off' run so the effect is directly attributable
The taxonomy lets them quantify which mechanism actually drives the measured improvement

slides.title: Anchoring dominates -- by more than 14x
slides.body: Across the labeled trials, procedural anchoring (the skill locks in a fixed sequence of steps) explains most of the wins. Explicit knowledge injection (the skill teaches a fact the model lacked) is rare by comparison.
bullets: A distilled SKILL.md procedure beat keeping the full raw trajectory (Workflow Memory) by 6.06 points in matched comparisons
That gap holds even though Workflow Memory contains strictly more information -- compression into a clean procedure is what helps

slides.title: A deploy checklist beats a deploy explanation
slides.body: Picture two versions of the same skill for a 'deploy this service' task. One is a paragraph explaining the deployment architecture. The other is a numbered checklist: build, run tests, health-check, promote, verify.
bullets: Without any skill, the agent improvises the order and skips steps like the health check inconsistently across runs
The paragraph-style skill (knowledge injection) barely changes the failure rate -- the model already 'knew' the architecture
The checklist-style skill (procedural anchoring) makes the agent follow the same steps every run, which is where the reliability gain actually comes from

slides.title: The library gets bigger, the right skill gets harder to find
slides.body: The paper's second major finding is a retrieval bottleneck: even a perfect skill is useless if the agent can't reliably retrieve and actually use it once the library grows.
bullets: Actual-use precision falls from 29.6% (pool of 5 skills) to 3.3% (pool of 100 skills)
Skills also fail outright under brittle assumptions, incompatible contexts, or when the situation needs adaptation the fixed procedure doesn't cover
Bigger skill libraries aren't free -- they trade coverage for a much harder retrieval problem

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Skills aren't a knowledge-injection trick -- they're a behavior-stabilization trick, and that changes how you should write and manage them.
bullets: Write skills as procedures/checklists, not explanations -- that's the mechanism doing the actual work
Distill trajectories into clean SKILL.md files rather than dumping raw execution history
Keep libraries small and curated: retrieval precision collapses well before 100 skills
Test each skill across contexts before trusting it broadly -- brittle assumptions are the main failure mode

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what's the dominant mechanism by which skills help agents succeed?
options: Injecting facts the base model didn't already know
Procedural anchoring -- stabilizing the sequence of actions taken
Increasing the model's effective context window
Fine-tuning the base model's weights
questions.explanation: Procedural anchoring accounted for 65.7% of cases where a skill helped, versus just 4.5% for explicit knowledge injection -- skills mostly work by locking in a reliable sequence of steps, not by teaching new facts.

questions.prompt: What happened to actual-use retrieval precision as the skill library grew from 5 to 100 skills?
options: It stayed roughly flat
It fell from 29.6% to 3.3%
It rose from 3.3% to 29.6%
It doubled
questions.explanation: Precision collapsed from 29.6% at a pool of 5 skills to 3.3% at a pool of 100 -- a real scaling bottleneck: bigger libraries make it much harder for the agent to actually find and use the right skill.

questions.prompt: How did a distilled SKILL.md procedure compare to keeping the full raw trajectory (Workflow Memory)?
options: It underperformed by 6.06 points
It outperformed by 6.06 points, despite containing less raw detail
The two were statistically identical
Workflow Memory isn't a valid comparison
questions.explanation: The distilled skill beat Workflow Memory by 6.06 points in matched comparisons -- evidence that compressing a trajectory into a clean procedure helps more than preserving every execution detail.

posts.title: Mistral's Agentic Search: Retrieval That Opens Documents
posts.subtitle: From one-shot top-k to a five-action retrieval loop
posts.summary: Mistral AI's Agentic Search, announced August 20, 2026, replaces one-shot top-k chunk retrieval with a five-action loop -- search, open, navigate, read, grep -- that lets a model inspect and follow references across a corpus before answering. On Mistral's own benchmarks it triples FinanceBench correctness (26.7% to 86%) and cuts p90 latency on the same benchmark from 255s to 154s.

slides.title: Retrieval Gets a Researcher's Toolkit Instead of a Lookup Table
slides.body: Mistral AI announced Agentic Search on August 20, 2026 -- a retrieval layer that gives models five actions to inspect, navigate, and verify information across documents, instead of answering off a single fixed set of retrieved chunks.

slides.title: The answer isn't always in the first chunk
slides.body: Standard RAG embeds a query, pulls the top-k nearest chunks, and answers from whatever came back. When the real answer is buried on page 40 of a filing or requires cross-referencing two documents, that one-shot retrieval just fails.
bullets: A missed first retrieval means either a wrong answer or a blind re-search with a reformulated query
The model can never open a partially-matched document to look around it -- chunks are the only unit it sees
This hits long, table-heavy, or multi-document corpora hardest: financial filings, technical manuals, office documents

slides.title: Five actions: search, open, navigate, read, grep
slides.body: Agentic Search turns retrieval into a multi-step loop the model drives itself, rather than a single vector lookup executed once before generation.
bullets: search finds candidate sources; open inspects one directly; navigate moves through nearby chunks
grep finds exact terms inside a document; read pulls the resolved content into context
The model can refine queries and follow references before answering, without re-fetching chunks it's already seen

slides.title: Roughly 3x correctness on financial filings
slides.body: Mistral's own benchmark numbers show the biggest gains where naive top-k retrieval struggles most: dense, multi-document, table-heavy sources.
bullets: FinanceBench correctness roughly triples: 26.7% to 86%
OfficeQA Pro (table-heavy, multi-doc questions) gains 45.6 points: 6.3% to 51.9%

slides.title: Finding a buried covenant in a 10-K
slides.body: Ask 'what's the leverage covenant in this credit agreement' and a naive RAG system retrieves a chunk that mentions 'covenant' in passing on page 3 -- the wrong one.
bullets: Agentic Search's search step finds the credit agreement document rather than a single chunk
open + navigate move it to the covenants section instead of trusting the first embedding match
grep locates the exact defined term, and read pulls the precise clause into context before answering

slides.title: More steps, but not more latency
slides.body: A multi-step retrieval loop sounds slower, but Mistral reports the opposite on FinanceBench -- because it stops the model from repeatedly failing and blindly re-searching.
bullets: p90 latency drops from 255s to 154s, and mean latency from 108s to 71s on FinanceBench
The rollout is currently tied to Mistral's own stack: the Search Toolkit for custom deployments, or built into Libraries in Studio and Vibe
It still depends on sources being structured enough for 'open' and 'navigate' to mean something -- unstructured or poorly indexed corpora limit the benefit

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Agentic Search reframes retrieval as an action space the model operates, not a single vector lookup that happens before generation starts.
bullets: Biggest wins show up on long, multi-document, or table-heavy sources where the answer isn't in the first hit
Five actions -- search, open, navigate, read, grep -- let the model verify before answering instead of guessing from one chunk
Latency can improve even with more steps, by cutting failed one-shot retrievals and blind re-searches
Currently ships through Mistral's own Search Toolkit, Studio, and Vibe products

questions.prompt: What core limitation of standard RAG does Agentic Search target?
options: Models can't generate vector embeddings
The model can only answer from a fixed set of top-k chunks and can't inspect or navigate beyond them
RAG systems can't support English-language documents
Standard RAG is too fast to be accurate
questions.explanation: Standard RAG retrieves a fixed top-k set of chunks once and answers from that. If the real answer isn't in those chunks, the model has no way to open or navigate the document further -- exactly the gap Agentic Search fills.

questions.prompt: What five actions does Agentic Search give the model?
options: Train, fine-tune, deploy, monitor, log
Search, open, navigate, read, grep
Embed, index, rank, filter, cache
Plan, act, observe, reflect, retry
questions.explanation: The five actions -- search, open, navigate, read, grep -- let the model treat retrieval as a multi-step investigation instead of a single lookup, inspecting and following references before answering.

questions.prompt: On FinanceBench, what happened to both correctness and latency after Agentic Search was applied?
options: Correctness rose (26.7% to 86%) and latency fell (p90 255s to 154s)
Correctness rose but latency got much worse
Both correctness and latency stayed flat
Correctness fell while latency improved
questions.explanation: Mistral reported correctness roughly tripling (26.7% to 86%) while p90 latency dropped from 255s to 154s -- the multi-step loop avoids the repeated failed retrievals that made one-shot RAG both slower and less accurate.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Capacity Without the Compute Bill
posts.subtitle: Why the biggest open models route instead of running everything
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces a transformer's dense feed-forward layer with many smaller expert networks and a router that activates only a few per token. That decouples total model capacity from per-token compute, letting models like Mixtral and today's largest open-weight releases scale parameters far past what a dense model could afford to run -- at the cost of holding every expert in memory and solving a genuinely hard load-balancing problem.

slides.title: MoE: Bigger Model, Same Compute Per Token
slides.body: Dense transformers spend every parameter on every token. Mixture of Experts swaps the single feed-forward block for many specialized experts plus a router that activates only a handful -- so total capacity can grow 10x while compute per token barely moves.

slides.title: Dense scaling means every extra parameter costs FLOPs
slides.body: In a standard dense transformer, doubling the parameter count roughly doubles the FLOPs needed per token, at both training and inference time -- there's no way to add capacity without paying for it on every single forward pass.
bullets: Most of what a given token needs is probably encoded in a small slice of a huge parameter set
But a dense layer runs 100% of its weights on 100% of tokens regardless
That coupling between total capacity and per-token cost is the thing MoE breaks

slides.title: A router picks k experts out of N, per token
slides.body: Replace the dense feed-forward layer with N smaller expert FFNs and a lightweight router (a linear layer plus softmax) trained end-to-end with the rest of the model. For each token, the router selects the top-k experts, runs only those, and combines their outputs.
bullets: Total parameters = the sum of all N experts (the model's capacity)
Active parameters per token = just the k selected experts, typically k=1 or k=2
Mixtral 8x7B, for example, uses 8 experts with top-2 routing -- 2 of 8 run per token

slides.title: Capacity of a big dense model, compute of a small one
slides.body: Mixtral 8x7B has roughly 47B total parameters split across 8 experts, but only about 13B are active for any given token (2 experts plus shared attention and embedding layers) -- inference cost tracks the smaller number.
bullets: The gap between total and active parameters is exactly what MoE buys you

slides.title: Watching one token get routed
slides.body: A batch mixes a line of Python with a sentence of English prose. Neither token type was hand-assigned to an expert -- specialization emerges from training because it lowers the loss.
bullets: The token embedding hits the router, which outputs a score for each of the N experts
Softmax over those scores picks the top-k -- say, the code token routes to experts 3 and 6, the prose token to experts 1 and 4
Each selected expert runs its own FFN; their outputs are combined, weighted by the router's own probabilities
Over training, expert 3 or 6 may drift toward handling syntax-heavy tokens simply because that reduced loss more often

slides.title: You save compute, not memory -- and routing can collapse
slides.body: MoE's savings are specifically in FLOPs per token. Every expert still has to be loaded somewhere, so total memory footprint tracks the full parameter count, not the active subset.
bullets: Without an auxiliary load-balancing loss, the router can collapse onto using just a few experts, wasting the rest of the model's capacity
Serving needs expert parallelism across GPUs with all-to-all communication to route tokens -- real infrastructure complexity
Batch efficiency drops when tokens in a batch scatter across many different experts, hurting hardware utilization versus dense models at small batch sizes
Gains concentrate at high-throughput, well-batched serving -- less compelling for single-request, low-latency use

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MoE is the architectural trick behind why today's largest open-weight models can pack far more parameters than a dense model could ever afford to run.
bullets: A router activates only k of N experts per token, decoupling total capacity from per-token compute
You pay in memory (every expert must be resident) and serving complexity (routing, load balancing, expert parallelism), not in FLOPs per token
Load-balancing losses are essential -- without them, routing collapses onto a handful of experts
Best fit: large-scale, high-throughput serving where you can batch well and shard experts across enough devices to hold them all

questions.prompt: What does a Mixture-of-Experts router actually decide?
options: Which transformer layer to skip entirely
Which k experts process a given token
How many tokens the model will generate
Which GPU a request gets scheduled on
questions.explanation: The router is a small learned gate that scores every expert for a given token and selects the top-k to actually run -- that's the core mechanism that separates MoE from a dense feed-forward layer.

questions.prompt: In Mixtral 8x7B (8 experts, top-2 routing, ~47B total parameters), roughly how many parameters are active per token?
options: ~47B -- all of them run every time
~13B -- only 2 experts plus shared layers run
~7B -- exactly one expert's worth
~1B -- just the router itself
questions.explanation: Only 2 of the 8 experts run per token, plus shared attention and embedding layers, so active compute lands around 13B parameters even though total capacity is roughly 47B.

questions.prompt: What's the main hidden cost of MoE that a dense model of the same active size doesn't have?
options: It requires far more training data than any dense model
Every expert must still be held in memory even though only a few run per token, plus routing and load-balancing complexity
It cannot run on GPUs at all
It only works for image and video models
questions.explanation: MoE saves FLOPs per token, not memory -- all experts must be resident somewhere, and serving requires expert-parallel infrastructure plus a load-balancing loss to keep the router from collapsing onto a handful of experts.

posts.title: Reflexion: Learning From Failure Without Retraining
posts.subtitle: A verbal note to itself replaces the gradient update
posts.summary: Reflexion wraps a frozen LLM in an Actor / Evaluator / Self-Reflection loop: the Evaluator scores a trajectory, Self-Reflection turns that signal into a specific verbal critique, and the critique is stored in memory for the next attempt -- no weight updates required. On HumanEval it pushed GPT-4's pass@1 from 80% to 91%, and on ALFWorld it solved 130/134 tasks against a plain ReAct baseline.

slides.title: An agent that critiques its own failure, then tries again
slides.body: Reflexion skips gradient updates entirely. Instead of retraining, the agent writes itself a note about what went wrong and carries that note into the next attempt.

slides.title: Fine-tuning after every failure is too slow to use mid-task
slides.body: Traditional RL turns a failure into a gradient update -- useful across many training episodes, but useless for an agent that needs to do better on its very next attempt, in the same session.
bullets: A weight update needs a gradient computation and a training loop -- not something you can run between two tool calls
A single failed trajectory carries a specific lesson ("called the API with the wrong key name") that a scalar reward collapses into one number
Naive retry-until-success wastes the failure entirely -- nothing stops the agent from repeating the same mistake

slides.title: Three roles: Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection
slides.body: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) wraps a frozen LLM in a loop of three roles that never touch its weights.
bullets: Actor: the base LLM produces a trajectory -- actions, code, or reasoning steps -- given the task and any prior reflections
Evaluator: scores that trajectory -- unit tests for code, exact-match for QA, environment success/fail for decision-making tasks
Self-Reflection model: turns the Evaluator's signal into a specific verbal critique instead of a bare pass/fail number

slides.title: The critique is stored, not just spoken
slides.body: Each reflection is appended to a small episodic memory buffer that gets injected into the Actor's context on the next trial.
bullets: The memory buffer is capped -- the paper keeps roughly the last 1-3 reflections, since it has to fit in the context window, not a database
No parameters change between trials -- every improvement lives entirely in the text carried forward
The loop repeats for a fixed trial budget (up to ~10-12 trials in the paper) or until the Evaluator reports success

slides.title: HumanEval: 80% to 91% pass@1, with no retraining
slides.body: On the HumanEval coding benchmark, wrapping GPT-4 in the Reflexion loop pushed pass@1 past the prior state of the art -- purely through self-critique and retries on the same problem.
bullets: Baseline GPT-4, zero-shot, no reflection: 80% pass@1 -- the state of the art at publication
GPT-4 + Reflexion: 91% pass@1 -- unit-test failures become the Evaluator signal that drives the next reflection
On ALFWorld's 134 decision-making tasks, Reflexion solved 130 versus a plain ReAct baseline, and cut hallucinated-action rates from 32% to 3% over 10 trials

slides.title: Reflexion vs. plain retry vs. RL fine-tuning
It only works when there's a real evaluator
slides.body: Reflexion's whole loop depends on getting back a trustworthy pass/fail or reward signal -- weak or absent evaluators break it.
bullets: Tasks without a checkable signal, like open-ended creative writing, give the Self-Reflection model nothing solid to critique
An LLM-judged Evaluator can itself hallucinate a wrong verdict, teaching the agent the wrong lesson with total confidence
The memory buffer's small cap means older, still-relevant lessons get pushed out as new trials accumulate
Each trial costs a full extra generation pass -- multiply that by the trial budget before assuming it's cheap

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Reflexion adds a learning loop entirely in-context, with no training infrastructure required.
bullets: Actor generates, Evaluator scores, Self-Reflection writes a specific verbal lesson, memory carries it into the next trial
No gradient updates -- the thing that 'improves' is the growing text in the prompt, not the model's weights
It needs a real evaluator signal (unit tests, exact-match, environment success) -- a bad evaluator teaches a bad lesson
Proven on coding (HumanEval 80% -> 91% pass@1) and decision-making (ALFWorld 130/134 tasks, hallucination rate 32% -> 3%)

questions.prompt: What does the Self-Reflection component actually produce?
options: A scalar reward value
A specific verbal critique stored in memory
An updated set of model weights
A new fine-tuning dataset
questions.explanation: Self-Reflection turns the Evaluator's pass/fail signal into a specific natural-language lesson, appended to the episodic memory buffer -- not a weight update.

questions.prompt: On HumanEval, what pass@1 score did GPT-4 + Reflexion reach, up from an 80% baseline?
questions.explanation: Reflexion pushed GPT-4 from 80% to 91% pass@1, purely by having it read its own unit-test failures and retry with a specific critique carried in context.

questions.prompt: Why does Reflexion break down on a task with no reliable evaluator?
options: Because the episodic memory buffer requires a database
Because the Self-Reflection model has nothing accurate to critique without a trustworthy pass/fail or reward signal
Because the Actor can't generate text without gradient updates
Because it requires a GPU to run the Evaluator
questions.explanation: The whole loop hinges on the Evaluator's signal. Without a trustworthy pass/fail or reward, Self-Reflection has nothing solid to critique and can reinforce the wrong lesson with full confidence.

posts.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: A New Scaling Axis for Agents
posts.subtitle: Score trajectories with logit expectations, not a single judge call
posts.summary: A Stanford team reframes verification -- deciding whether an agent's output is actually correct -- as its own scaling axis, separate from generation. By replacing a single discrete judge score with the expectation over scoring-token logits, LLM-as-a-Verifier scales along granularity, repeated evaluation, and criteria decomposition, pushing Terminal-Bench V2 from an 83.1% baseline to a new state of the art of 86.5% with no extra training.

slides.title: Verification deserves its own scaling curve
slides.body: Most agentic pipelines pick the best of several candidate solutions using an LLM judge that returns a single discrete score. LLM-as-a-Verifier argues that's leaving performance on the table -- verification itself scales, the same way generation does.

slides.title: A discrete 1-10 score throws away the model's own uncertainty
slides.body: When you ask an LLM judge to output a single number, you force it to collapse a distribution of belief into one token. Two trajectories the model is 55% vs. 95% confident about can round to the same discrete score.
bullets: Standard LM-as-a-judge samples one scoring token per candidate -- noisy, hard to compare precisely
Verification quality directly caps how well you can pick among agent trajectories, rerank samples, or train a reward signal
No amount of better generation fixes a bottlenecked verifier that keeps choosing the wrong winner

slides.title: Take the expectation over the logits, not a sample
slides.body: Instead of sampling a discrete judgment token, the verifier reads the full probability distribution over the scoring vocabulary (e.g., tokens '1' through '10') and computes its expected value. The result is a continuous score that captures exactly how confident the model actually is.
bullets: No extra training: works on top of any model that exposes token-level logits
A continuous score is directly comparable across candidates, not just orderable
Turns judging from 'pick a bucket' into 'read the belief distribution already inside the model'

slides.title: Three independent knobs to scale verification
slides.body: Because the score is now continuous, the framework can improve it the same way you'd scale test-time compute for generation -- along three separate axes.
bullets: Granularity (G): score on a finer scale (more possible values) instead of a coarse pass/fail
Repeated evaluation (K): sample the verification itself multiple times and average, reducing variance
Criteria decomposition: split one holistic judgment into several sub-criteria, score each, then ensemble

slides.title: Each axis moves the needle on its own
slides.body: On 200 sampled Terminal-Bench 2.0 trajectories, the authors varied one axis at a time and measured verification accuracy against ground truth.
bullets: Granularity: 73.1% at G=1 -> 77.5% at G=20
Repeated evaluation: 74.7% at K=1 -> 77.4% at K=16
Criteria decomposition: 75.2-76.4% for any single criterion alone -> 78.3% once three criteria are ensembled

slides.title: State of the art across four different agent benchmarks
slides.body: Plugged into an agentic coding harness on Terminal-Bench V2, the verifier lifts accuracy from an 83.1% baseline to 86.5% -- ahead of every other model-and-harness combination the authors tested.
bullets: Also sets new marks on SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%) -- coding, robotics, and medical agents alike

slides.title: The cost is inference compute, and it needs open logits
slides.body: Scaling K and criteria decomposition means running the verifier many more times per candidate -- real added latency and cost at inference time, not training time. The technique also assumes access to token-level logit distributions, which some closed API tiers don't expose.
bullets: Gains are front-loaded: granularity and repeated evaluation both show diminishing returns past a point
Not a replacement for a trained reward model when you already have abundant labeled preference data
Best fit: settings where you can't or don't want to train a dedicated verifier, and can afford extra inference passes

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Verification is not a fixed judge you bolt on at the end -- it's a resource you can spend more of, in three different ways, to buy real accuracy.
bullets: Replace discrete judge scores with the expectation over scoring-token logits when the API exposes them
Scale granularity, repeated evaluation, and criteria decomposition independently, then combine them
Expect the biggest wins from ensembling sub-criteria, not just cranking up one axis alone
Treat it as a training-free lever for agentic pipelines already bottlenecked on picking the right trajectory

questions.prompt: What does LLM-as-a-Verifier compute instead of a single sampled judgment token?
options: A majority vote across three separate models
The expectation over the logit distribution of scoring tokens
A fine-tuned regression head bolted onto the base model
An average of human ratings collected via crowdsourcing
questions.explanation: Instead of sampling one discrete score, the verifier reads the model's full probability distribution over the scoring tokens and takes its expected value -- a continuous score with no extra training required.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three scaling axes the paper introduces?
options: Granularity of the scoring scale
Repeated evaluation, averaged
Criteria decomposition into sub-scores
Fine-tuning the verifier on labeled preference pairs
questions.explanation: The three axes are granularity (G), repeated evaluation (K), and criteria decomposition. Fine-tuning on preference pairs is the alternative the paper explicitly avoids -- it's a training-free technique.

questions.prompt: On Terminal-Bench V2, what did LLM-as-a-Verifier improve accuracy from and to?
questions.explanation: The paper reports lifting Terminal-Bench V2 accuracy from an 83.1% discrete-judge baseline to 86.5%, ahead of every other model-and-harness combination tested, including GPT-5.5 + NexAU-AHE at 84.7%.

posts.title: Jalapeño: OpenAI's First Chip Takes Aim at Nvidia
posts.subtitle: 700 watts, custom silicon, and a benchmark to prove it
posts.summary: OpenAI published its first independent benchmark results for Jalapeño, the custom inference ASIC it co-designed with Broadcom, claiming up to 1.9x more performance per watt and up to 3.6x lower latency than Nvidia's current GB200/GB300 systems. It's OpenAI's clearest move yet toward controlling its own inference stack rather than depending entirely on Nvidia GPUs.

slides.title: OpenAI's first chip has numbers to back it up
slides.body: Announced in June 2026, Jalapeño is OpenAI's first custom AI accelerator, co-designed with Broadcom specifically for inference rather than training. On August 26, OpenAI published its first independent benchmark results.

slides.title: Nvidia GPUs are general-purpose; inference at OpenAI's scale isn't
slides.body: Training and inference have very different hardware needs -- inference is dominated by memory bandwidth and latency, not raw matmul throughput. Renting that efficiency from a general-purpose GPU means paying for flexibility OpenAI doesn't need once a model is deployed at scale.
bullets: OpenAI serves hundreds of millions of ChatGPT requests against a small set of models -- a case for specialization
Nvidia GPUs remain OpenAI's primary supply; this isn't a replacement, it's a second source
Every point of efficiency gained at inference compounds across OpenAI's entire serving fleet

slides.title: OpenAI designed it; Broadcom and Celestica built it
slides.body: Jalapeño is an OpenAI-designed accelerator: Broadcom contributed the silicon implementation plus its Tomahawk networking and switch fabric, while Celestica handled board, rack, and system integration.
bullets: Rated at 700W, but sustained 550W or less during the published tests
Uses newer HBM4 memory -- a generation ahead of the Nvidia GB200/GB300 it was benchmarked against
OpenAI plans to start deploying it inside its own infrastructure by the end of 2026

slides.title: 1.5-1.9x more performance per watt on InferenceX
slides.body: OpenAI ran the InferenceX benchmark suite (an independent standard from SemiAnalysis) across three large models, comparing Jalapeño to Nvidia's GB200/GB300 systems.

slides.title: Worked scenario: serving a 670B open model
slides.body: One of the three models OpenAI benchmarked, DeepSeek R1 670B, isn't even one of its own -- a deliberate choice to show the efficiency gain isn't tuned only for OpenAI's internal models. Running it, Jalapeño's latency advantage over GB200/GB300 fell within the reported 1.7x-3.6x band, meaning the same request could resolve markedly faster at a lower power draw.
bullets: Testing on non-OpenAI models is meant to show the efficiency gain is architectural, not a benchmark trick
Lower latency at the same or lower power directly cuts the cost of serving every chat completion
None of the three test models were trained specifically for this chip

slides.title: The comparison isn't fully apples-to-apples yet
slides.body: Independent analysts (SemiAnalysis) noted the test is somewhat unfair to Nvidia: Jalapeño ships with newer HBM4 memory that GB200/GB300 don't have. Nvidia's own upcoming Rubin platform also uses HBM4 and would be the fairer like-for-like comparison once it ships.
bullets: A memory-generation advantage inflates the apparent gap versus current-gen Nvidia hardware
OpenAI is not dropping Nvidia -- it explicitly plans to keep deploying GPUs from Nvidia and other suppliers alongside Jalapeño
Real-world gains depend on how the chip performs once it's actually serving production traffic, not just a benchmark suite

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Jalapeño is OpenAI's opening move into owning its own inference silicon -- a hedge against Nvidia dependency and pricing, backed by a real independent benchmark rather than just a slide deck.
bullets: 1.5-1.9x perf-per-watt and 1.7-3.6x lower latency than Nvidia GB200/GB300 on InferenceX, across three large models
Co-designed with Broadcom (silicon, networking) and Celestica (systems) -- OpenAI owns the architecture, not the fab
Deployment inside OpenAI's own infrastructure is planned by end of 2026, alongside continued Nvidia and other suppliers
Treat the numbers as directionally real but not yet apples-to-apples versus Nvidia's next-gen Rubin

questions.prompt: What kind of workload is Jalapeño specifically designed for?
options: Training frontier models from scratch
Inference / serving already-trained models
Video game rendering
On-device mobile inference
questions.explanation: Jalapeño is built specifically for LLM inference and serving, not training -- a different set of hardware tradeoffs dominated by memory bandwidth and latency rather than raw training throughput.

posts.title: Orchestrator-Worker: One Agent Plans, Many Execute
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's pattern for tasks you can't pre-plan
posts.summary: The orchestrator-worker pattern is one of Anthropic's core agent workflows: a lead agent dynamically decomposes a task, delegates pieces to parallel subagents it spins up on the fly, and synthesizes their results. Anthropic's own multi-agent research system uses exactly this pattern and reports a 90.2% improvement over a single-agent baseline -- at the cost of roughly 15x more tokens.

slides.title: When you can't predict the subtasks in advance
slides.body: Parallelization workflows split a task into subtasks you define ahead of time. Orchestrator-worker is for the harder case: a lead agent looks at the input and decides, on the fly, what the subtasks even are.

slides.title: A single agent's context window is the bottleneck
slides.body: Open-ended research or broad exploration tasks can require reading far more source material than fits in one context window, and the branches worth exploring aren't known until you're partway through.
bullets: One agent chasing every lead sequentially burns time and loses earlier context to compaction
Pre-defining subtasks, like a fixed parallelization split, doesn't work when the right subtasks depend on what's found
Some domains -- breadth-first research, competitive analysis, literature review -- are naturally made of independent, parallel threads

slides.title: A lead agent plans, spins up subagents, and synthesizes
slides.body: The orchestrator (lead agent) reads the task, decomposes it into a number of independent subtasks it decides in the moment, and dispatches each to a fresh subagent running in parallel with its own context window.
bullets: Each subagent needs an explicit objective, expected output format, tool/source guidance, and clear task boundaries
Subagents work simultaneously, not one after another -- wall-clock time doesn't scale with subtask count
The orchestrator collects every subagent's output and synthesizes a single final answer, often through a separate citation/verification pass

slides.title: Anthropic's own research system, in numbers
slides.body: Anthropic's multi-agent Research feature is built exactly this way: a lead agent coordinates 3-5 subagents that each explore a different angle of the query in parallel.
bullets: Measured 90.2% better performance than a single-agent Claude baseline on internal research evaluations
Token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance in performance across configurations
But it uses roughly 15x more tokens than a single chat turn to get there

slides.title: Orchestrator-worker vs. plain parallelization

rows: Task shape is known ahead of time
Task shape only emerges while working
Lead agent synthesizes all subagent outputs

slides.title: It's expensive, and it's a bad fit for tightly coupled work
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit that this pattern is not for every task. Multi-agent systems excel at problems that split into independent, parallel strands -- they're a poor fit for anything where the work is tightly interdependent.
bullets: Most coding tasks fail here: file A's changes usually depend on what the agent working on file B just did
The ~15x token multiplier only pays off when the task's value clearly exceeds that extra cost -- legal due diligence, competitive intel, literature review
Debugging is harder: a wrong final answer could trace back to any of several parallel subagents

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Orchestrator-worker trades tokens and coordination complexity for the ability to tackle tasks whose shape you can't know in advance.
bullets: Use it for breadth-first, independent-strand work: research, competitive analysis, broad literature review
Give every subagent an explicit objective, output format, tool guidance, and boundaries -- vague delegation compounds errors
Skip it for tightly interdependent work like most coding, where shared real-time context matters more than parallelism
Budget for roughly an order of magnitude more tokens than a single-agent approach, and confirm the task's value justifies it

questions.prompt: What distinguishes orchestrator-worker from plain parallelization?
options: Orchestrator-worker never runs subagents at the same time

Parallelization requires more tokens
Orchestrator-worker has no lead agent
questions.explanation: Parallelization splits a task into pre-defined subtasks. Orchestrator-worker's lead agent decides what the subtasks are on the fly, based on what the input actually requires.

options: About 2x
About 15x
About 100x

questions.explanation: Anthropic reported multi-agent systems use roughly 15x more tokens than a single chat turn -- a real cost that only pays off when the task's value clearly exceeds it.

options: Coding agents can't use tools

Coding tasks are typically tightly interdependent, requiring shared real-time context between changes

questions.explanation: The pattern works best on independent, parallel strands of work. Most coding tasks are tightly coupled -- a change in one file often depends on what's happening in another -- which needs shared context, not isolated parallel subagents.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: When the Server Needs to Ask You Something
posts.subtitle: Mid-task, structured, and never for secrets
posts.summary: Elicitation is the MCP primitive that lets a server pause mid-execution and ask the user a structured question through the client, instead of guessing or failing. It fills the gap left by MCP's other primitives — tools, resources, prompts, sampling — none of which handle 'I need one more piece of information from a human before I can finish.'

slides.title: The primitive for 'wait, I need to ask you something'
slides.body: MCP gives servers tools to call, resources to expose, prompts to template, and sampling to request completions from the model. Elicitation, added in the 2025-06-18 spec, is the missing piece: a way for a server to request structured input from the human user, mid-task.

slides.title: Without it, servers either guess or crash
slides.body: A booking tool that needs a departure city the user forgot to mention has two bad options without elicitation: guess (and risk being wrong) or throw an error and force the user to restart the whole request with more detail.
bullets: Tool calls are one-shot: no built-in way to ask a follow-up mid-call
Forcing users to front-load every possible parameter makes prompts brittle
Failing and restarting loses all the context already gathered

slides.title: elicitation/create: a request with a JSON Schema attached
slides.body: A server sends an elicitation/create request carrying a message and a requestedSchema. The client renders a form (or equivalent UI) from that schema, collects the user's answer, and returns it — all before the server's original task resumes.
bullets: requestedSchema uses a restricted subset of JSON Schema — flat fields, not deeply nested objects
The client, not the server, controls how the prompt is actually shown to the user
The server pauses and waits; execution resumes once the client responds

slides.title: Where it fits among MCP's primitives
slides.body: Elicitation is client-side capability, like sampling — the server can only use it if the client declares support during initialization. That keeps clients in control of what user-facing interruptions are allowed to happen.
bullets: Tools: server exposes actions the model can invoke
Resources: server exposes data the client can read
Sampling: server asks the client's model for a completion
Elicitation: server asks the client's human user for input

slides.title: Worked example: a flight-booking server
slides.body: User: 'Book me a flight to Tokyo next week.' The server has enough to search flights but not enough to book — it doesn't know the user's seat preference or which of three matching flights they want. Instead of erroring out, it elicits: sends a schema with an enum of the three flight options and a seat-preference field, the client renders it as a picker, and the user's answer flows straight back into the same booking call.
bullets: No restart: the search results already gathered aren't thrown away
The schema constrains the answer to valid choices, not free text the server has to re-parse
One elicitation round-trip instead of an entire new conversational turn

slides.title: The rule the spec is explicit about: never for secrets
slides.body: The MCP spec states servers MUST NOT use elicitation to request sensitive information — no passwords, API keys, or payment details through this channel. For anything sensitive, the correct pattern is to direct the user to an external URL that bypasses the MCP client entirely.
bullets: Elicitation payloads pass through the client and potentially the model's context
Sensitive data belongs in an out-of-band flow (OAuth redirect, hosted checkout page), not a schema field
Clients are expected to show users exactly what's being asked and let them decline

slides.title: Elicitation vs. just asking the model to ask a clarifying question
slides.body: You could get similar behavior by having the model itself ask a clarifying question in chat — but that's unstructured and easy for the model to skip or mis-parse. Elicitation makes the ask structured and enforced by schema.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Elicitation closes MCP's last gap between 'server has almost enough to finish' and 'server actually finishes' — without falling back to guesswork or a hard failure.
bullets: Use it for missing non-sensitive parameters a tool call needs mid-execution
Never use it for credentials or payment data — route those out-of-band
It's a client-declared capability: servers must check support before relying on it
The restricted JSON Schema subset trades expressiveness for guaranteed-renderable UI

questions.prompt: What problem does MCP elicitation solve that tools, resources, and sampling don't?
options: Letting a server expose static data files
Letting a server request a model completion
Letting a server pause mid-task and request structured input directly from the human user
Letting a server cache previous responses
questions.explanation: Tools, resources, and sampling cover actions, data, and model completions respectively. Elicitation is specifically for when the server needs something only the human user can supply, mid-execution.

questions.prompt: What does the MCP spec explicitly forbid servers from doing with elicitation?
options: Asking for a seat preference
Requesting sensitive information like passwords or payment details
Using a JSON Schema to constrain the answer
Pausing execution while waiting for a response
questions.explanation: The spec states servers MUST NOT use elicitation for sensitive information. Anything sensitive should go through an out-of-band flow, like a redirect to an external URL, that doesn't pass through the MCP client.

questions.prompt: Why is elicitation a client-declared capability rather than something a server can always assume is available?
options: Because it requires a paid MCP tier
Because it only works with certain models
Because the client controls whether and how user-facing interruptions are allowed, so it must opt in during initialization
Because it's deprecated in favor of tools
questions.explanation: Like sampling, elicitation depends on the client agreeing to handle it — the client is the one rendering UI and mediating access to the human user, so it declares support up front rather than servers assuming it exists.

posts.title: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard: USB-C for AI Agents
posts.subtitle: Letting Claude run a microscope the same way it queries a database
posts.summary: On August 27, 2026, Anthropic previewed the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared, model-agnostic specification that lets AI agents operate physical lab and manufacturing equipment — microscopes, liquid handlers, robotic arms — the way MCP already lets them call software tools. It's in limited research preview with partners like AWS, Genentech, Universal Robots, and Danaher, with open-sourcing planned once safety work matures.

slides.title: MCP connected agents to software. MHS connects them to machines.
slides.body: Anthropic previewed the Model Hardware Standard on August 27, 2026 — an open specification for AI agents to operate physical devices, reachable over the Model Context Protocol, aimed first at scientific research and manufacturing hardware.

slides.title: Every lab instrument speaks its own dialect
slides.body: Before MHS, a microscope, a liquid handler, and a robotic arm each shipped with proprietary control software that didn't talk to the others — the same fragmentation MCP solved for software tools, but for physical devices.
bullets: No shared interface meant custom integration work per device, per vendor
Agents couldn't chain multiple instruments into one autonomous workflow
Anthropic frames it with the USB-C analogy: one connector standard instead of one per manufacturer

slides.title: A model-agnostic hardware layer, over MCP
slides.body: MHS is delivered as a specification, not a proprietary API — it's reachable over the Model Context Protocol and explicitly designed to work with any model, not just Claude, so labs aren't locked into one vendor's AI to use their own equipment.
bullets: Works with any device exposing a programmable interface
Supported device classes: liquid handlers, robotic arms, plate readers, microscopes, lasers, cameras, qPCR machines, centrifuges, incubators, sensors, and boards like Raspberry Pi
Currently a limited research preview; Anthropic plans to open-source it once further safety evaluation is complete

slides.title: What early partners actually did with it
slides.body: A Claude-based agent recalibrated a $700,000 laser on a QuEra quantum computer with 99.3% success across 700 trials. Genentech ran a protein assay without human intervention. The University of Washington connected six instruments in under a week. Carnegie Mellon set up a dose-response experiment from scratch in eight hours — about three times faster than the manual process.
bullets: QuEra: 99.3% success across 700 laser-calibration trials
Genentech: unattended protein assay execution
UW: six instruments wired together in under a week
CMU: dose-response experiment built from scratch in 8 hours, ~3x faster than manual

slides.title: MHS vs. MCP: same idea, different layer
slides.body: The two specs share a design philosophy but target different resources.

slides.title: Why this is riskier than software tool-calling
slides.body: A misfired API call can corrupt data; a misfired robotic arm or laser can damage six-figure equipment or injure someone. That's why MHS is shipping as a narrow research preview to vetted scientific and manufacturing partners rather than a public open-source release.
bullets: Physical actions are harder to undo than software actions
Preview partners are selected labs and manufacturers, not the general public
Open-sourcing is explicitly gated on further safety evaluation, not a fixed date

slides.title: The bigger picture
slides.body: MHS is Anthropic's clearest move yet from agents-that-write-code to agents-that-operate-things. If MCP's history is a guide — from Anthropic-only spec to industry-wide standard — MHS's real test is whether other labs and hardware vendors adopt it once it's public.
bullets: Physical-world agent control is the new frontier after software tool-calling
Model-agnostic design is a deliberate bet on broad adoption, not lock-in
Safety gating before open-sourcing sets a more cautious precedent than MCP's own launch

To keep it exclusive to Anthropic's own hardware
